questions.stem: Where does the novel's main action in August 1944 take place?
options: Normandy, on the beaches during the D-Day landings
Saint-Malo, a walled port in Brittany, under siege
Paris, as Allied troops and the Resistance free the city
Berlin, as Soviet troops close in on the German capital
questions.explanation: The novel keeps returning to the siege of Saint-Malo in August 1944, when American forces bombard the German-held city. Marie-Laure and Werner are both trapped there.

questions.stem: Why does Daniel LeBlanc build his daughter a model of their Paris neighbourhood?
options: So that he can hide the museum's spare keys inside its tiny houses
So that she can learn the streets by touch after she goes blind
So that she can stay safely indoors instead of walking the real streets
So that she can plan a route out of the city if the Germans invade
questions.explanation: Marie-Laure goes blind at six. Her father, the museum's locksmith, builds a model she can feel with her fingers until she can walk the real streets on her own.

questions.stem: How does Werner first become fascinated by radio?
options: He finds a broken radio as a child and repairs it, sharing it with Jutta
His father, a radio engineer, teaches him before he dies in an accident
A teacher at Schulpforta gives him a radio as a prize for his schoolwork
Frau Elena buys a radio so the orphans can hear the news from Berlin
questions.explanation: Werner and his sister Jutta are orphans in a coal-mining town. Werner repairs a broken radio, and at night they listen to a Frenchman's science broadcasts, which shape his love of learning.

questions.stem: How does Werner's path to the school at Schulpforta begin?
options: He volunteers for the army and is sent to the school to train
He repairs a Nazi official's radio, and the official recommends him
Frau Elena writes to the school to praise his talent for science
He informs on Frau Elena for listening to forbidden broadcasts
questions.explanation: Werner fixes the radio of Herr Siedler, a Nazi official, who arranges for him to sit the entrance exams. The school offers an escape from the mines, which is why Werner is so eager to go.

questions.stem: Why do Marie-Laure and her father leave Paris in 1940?
options: The German army is about to occupy the city
Her father has been dismissed by the museum
Her great-uncle has asked them to nurse him
The museum has been destroyed in a bombing
questions.explanation: As Germany invades France, the pair flee to Saint-Malo, to Marie-Laure's great-uncle Etienne. Daniel is carrying either the Sea of Flames or one of its copies.

questions.stem: What happens to Daniel LeBlanc after he leaves Saint-Malo to go back to Paris?
options: He returns the diamond to the museum and stays on there as its keeper
He is arrested and never returns, though a few of his letters reach her
He is killed by von Rumpel, who believes he is carrying the real diamond
He joins the Resistance in Paris and dies in the fighting for the city
questions.explanation: Daniel is arrested on suspicion of conspiracy and held as a prisoner. Marie-Laure receives only a few letters, and he never comes back, which leaves her waiting and hoping.

questions.stem: What happens to Frederick at Schulpforta?
options: He is sent to the front as punishment for refusing to follow orders
He runs away to Berlin with Werner and hides in his mother's apartment
He refuses to join in the cruelty and is later beaten until he is brain-damaged
He is expelled after Werner reports his disobedience to Commandant Bastian
questions.explanation: Frederick will not take part when the cadets are ordered to torment a prisoner. He is singled out and later so badly beaten that he is left brain-damaged, and Werner's failure to help him haunts him.

questions.stem: What is Werner's job once he is sent into the army?
options: Sending coded messages between Berlin and the generals at the front
Tracking illegal radio transmitters so their operators can be found
Building radio towers to broadcast Nazi propaganda into occupied France
Repairing damaged radios for German officers along the Atlantic coast
questions.explanation: Werner's unit, led by Volkheimer, hunts down illegal radio signals, and the people operating them are killed. His skill, once a source of wonder, becomes a tool of violence.

questions.stem: Why does Werner keep the Saint-Malo broadcasts secret from his unit?
options: He plans to trade what he has learned to von Rumpel for the diamond
He has been ordered to listen to them in secret by Commandant Bastian
He recognises the science broadcasts he loved as a child and protects them
He believes the signal is too weak and too short to be worth reporting
questions.explanation: The broadcasts from Etienne's house are the same ones Werner and Jutta heard as children. By hiding them, Werner commits his first real act of resistance, and it links him to Marie-Laure.

questions.stem: What does Marie-Laure broadcast from the attic during the siege?
options: News bulletins copied from the BBC for the people sheltering below
Readings from Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, and pleas for help
Her father's letters, read aloud in the hope that he will hear them
Weather reports for the Allied ships waiting off the coast of Brittany
questions.explanation: Trapped and alone, Marie-Laure reads Jules Verne's novel from her braille copy over the transmitter and asks for help. Werner, buried under a hotel, hears her voice.

questions.stem: How do Werner and Marie-Laure finally meet?
options: Marie-Laure walks to the hotel where Werner is trapped and digs him out
Werner reaches Etienne's house and kills von Rumpel, who is hunting her
Marie-Laure finds Werner wounded in the street and hides him in the cellar
Werner is ordered to arrest Etienne and finds Marie-Laure in the attic
questions.explanation: After escaping the collapsed hotel, Werner goes to the house and finds von Rumpel searching for the diamond. He kills him, then meets Marie-Laure and helps her leave the city safely.

questions.stem: What does Marie-Laure do with the Sea of Flames?
options: She hands it to the American soldiers who take control of the city
She sends it back to the museum in Paris with her great-uncle Etienne
She locks it in a grotto that floods at high tide, returning it to the sea
She gives it to Werner to carry safely out of the city when he leaves
questions.explanation: Legend says the curse ends only if the stone goes back to the sea. Marie-Laure places it in a sea grotto and locks the gate, so its final fate is left uncertain.

questions.stem: How does Werner die?
options: He is shot by von Rumpel during their standoff in Etienne's house
He is killed when the cellar of the Hotel of Bees collapses on him
He is executed by his own unit for hiding the Saint-Malo broadcasts
He steps on a landmine while ill and a prisoner of war
questions.explanation: Taken prisoner and very sick, Werner wanders away in a fever and is killed by a landmine. His death is sudden and pointless, which is part of the novel's view of war.

questions.stem: What happens in the 1974 section of the novel?
options: Jutta brings Marie-Laure the model house Werner carried, with a key inside
Marie-Laure goes back to the grotto in Saint-Malo and finds the diamond
Volkheimer visits Marie-Laure in Paris and tells her how Werner died
Etienne publishes the old science broadcasts as a book for children
questions.explanation: Volkheimer gives Jutta Werner's belongings, and she travels to meet Marie-Laure. Inside the little model house is the grotto key, but Marie-Laure never learns what became of the stone.

questions.stem: How is the novel structured?
options: Short chapters alternate between Marie-Laure and Werner
Two long halves tell first Marie-Laure's story and then Werner's
Marie-Laure narrates in the first person, looking back from 2014
Letters between Werner and Jutta tell the story in the order it happened
questions.explanation: Doerr cuts between the two characters in brief chapters. Scenes from the 1944 siege are interwoven with their earlier lives, which move forward from 1934.

questions.stem: Why does Doerr open with the siege of 1944 and then go back to 1934?
options: Readers see the violence first, so the childhood chapters feel safe and settled
Readers are told who owns the real diamond before the story begins
Readers know both will be in Saint-Malo, so suspense comes from how they converge
Readers learn Werner's fate at once, so the ending holds no surprises
questions.explanation: Placing both characters in the besieged city first creates a question the whole book answers: how did their paths lead here? Each earlier chapter moves them closer together.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Marie-Laure LeBlanc?
options: A French Resistance leader who works as a radio engineer
A German orphan who grows up in a coal-mining town
A museum scientist who studies precious gems and legends
A blind girl from Paris, the daughter of a museum locksmith
questions.explanation: Marie-Laure is blind from the age of six. She is curious, brave and resourceful, and her chapters are told through touch, sound and smell.

questions.stem: Who is Etienne LeBlanc?
options: A perfume seller who informs on his neighbours to the occupying army
Marie-Laure's great-uncle, a war veteran who has not left his house in years
Marie-Laure's cousin, a fisherman who hides Resistance radios in his boat
A German officer who lodges in the house and protects Marie-Laure
questions.explanation: Etienne was damaged by the First World War and is afraid to go outside. Through Marie-Laure and Madame Manec he slowly finds the courage to act, broadcasting for the Resistance.

questions.stem: What role does Madame Manec play?
options: Marie-Laure's teacher, who teaches her to read braille in Saint-Malo
A museum official who sends Daniel the orders to return to Paris
Werner's guardian, who runs the orphanage in the mining town
Etienne's housekeeper, who draws local women into resistance
questions.explanation: Madame Manec mothers Marie-Laure and pushes the fearful Etienne to resist the occupation. She dies of illness, and her courage passes to Marie-Laure and Etienne.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Jutta, Werner's sister?
options: She works with Frau Elena to hide Jewish children in the orphanage
She distrusts the Nazi ideas Werner is drawn into and acts as his conscience
She envies Werner's place at Schulpforta and tries to win one for herself
She joins the Nazi youth movement for girls and urges Werner to follow her
questions.explanation: Jutta questions what Werner is becoming and resents the school that takes him away. Her doubts frame the moral choices Werner keeps putting off.

questions.stem: What drives Reinhold von Rumpel's search for the Sea of Flames?
options: He is a museum thief who plans to sell the diamond to the Allies
He is a French collector who wants the diamond back for France
He is a Gestapo officer ordered to find Daniel LeBlanc's daughter
He is a dying gem expert who hopes the diamond will save his life
questions.explanation: Von Rumpel is a German sergeant major and gemologist with a fatal illness. The legend that the stone keeps its owner alive turns his search into a desperate obsession.

questions.stem: How does Volkheimer complicate the idea of a simple 'enemy soldier'?
options: He secretly helps the Resistance while pretending to hunt its radios
He hates Werner but saves him only because the army needs his skills
He takes part in killings, yet protects Werner and later seeks out Jutta
He refuses to hunt the radio operators and is demoted for it by his officers
questions.explanation: Volkheimer is huge and frightening and leads a unit that kills radio operators. Yet he looks after Werner and, decades later, brings Werner's belongings to Jutta, so he is both violent and loyal.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Werner's moral journey?
options: He goes along with the Nazi system for opportunity, then acts against it to save Marie-Laure
He embraces Nazi ideas at Schulpforta and keeps faith with them until he is taken prisoner
He resists the Nazis from the start and joins the army only to sabotage it from within
He openly defends Frederick at Schulpforta and is sent to the front as a punishment for it
questions.explanation: Werner stays silent at Schulpforta and serves in a unit that kills, because the system offers him a future. Hiding the broadcasts and saving Marie-Laure are his late attempts to act on his conscience.

questions.stem: What were Nazi schools like the one at Schulpforta designed to do?
options: Train boys to become the future elite of the Nazi state
Prepare boys for jobs in Germany's coal and steel industries
Teach boys foreign languages so they could work as diplomats
Give orphaned boys a free general education in the sciences
questions.explanation: These elite schools trained boys in discipline, physical toughness and Nazi ideology. Doerr shows how they demanded obedience and punished anyone who stood out.

questions.stem: What happened to Saint-Malo in August 1944?
options: Much of it was destroyed as American forces fought to take it
It was handed to the Allies without a fight after the D-Day landings
It was burned by the Germans as they retreated toward Paris and Berlin
It was freed by the Resistance before the American forces arrived
questions.explanation: Allied bombing and shelling ruined most of the old walled city during the siege. Doerr uses this real event as the point where his two stories meet.

questions.stem: Why does the Paris museum have copies made of the Sea of Flames in 1940?
options: To put a copy on display so visitors would not know the stone had gone
To give a copy to the German army so it would leave the museum alone
To confuse thieves, by sending the real stone and the copies away separately
To sell the copies and pay for the museum's collection to be moved south
questions.explanation: The real diamond and three copies are given to different men to carry out of Paris. Not even Daniel can be sure whether he holds the real one.

questions.stem: Why does Werner dread turning fifteen?
options: He will be sent away to Schulpforta and have to leave Jutta behind
He will have to leave Jutta behind and live with an aunt in Berlin
He will be called up for the army and sent straight to the front
He will be sent to work in the coal mines where his father died
questions.explanation: In Zollverein, orphaned boys go down the mines at fifteen, and Werner's father died there. His fear of the mines explains why Schulpforta seems like rescue.

questions.stem: Which idea does the title most directly point to?
options: That the wartime blackout hides the city's suffering from the world
That Marie-Laure's blindness is the central tragedy of the novel
That much of what shapes our lives, like radio waves, is unseen
That the blind see more clearly than sighted people in wartime
questions.explanation: The Frenchman's broadcasts teach that most light is invisible to the human eye. The title extends this to the invisible forces in the novel: radio, love, memory and moral choice.

questions.stem: How does the novel present the legend of the Sea of Flames' curse?
options: It reveals the curse was a museum story to keep visitors from touching it
It leaves the curse uncertain, inviting readers to weigh fate against chance
It confirms the curse is real, since misfortune follows each of its keepers
It shows the curse was invented by von Rumpel to frighten the LeBlancs
questions.explanation: Misfortune follows the stone, but every disaster also has an ordinary cause in the war. Daniel and Marie-Laure struggle to decide what to believe, and Doerr never settles it.

questions.stem: How does the novel invite readers to view its German characters?
options: As victims who bear no responsibility for what the Nazi state did
As heroes whose loyalty to their country excuses what they did
As individuals shaped by pressure and choice, not simply as enemies
As fanatics whose belief in Nazi ideas drives everything they do
questions.explanation: Werner, Jutta, Frederick and Volkheimer are drawn as complex people. Doerr shows the pressure on them without excusing what they do, which is why Werner's guilt matters.

questions.stem: What is the main effect of Doerr writing the novel in the present tense?
options: The story seems like a history lesson told by an outside expert
The characters can comment directly on events after the war ends
Events feel immediate, as if readers live each moment too
Readers know the narrator is looking back calmly from the year 2014
questions.explanation: Present tense makes even the 1934 chapters feel as if they are happening now. It adds tension to the siege, because no one, including the reader, knows what comes next.

questions.stem: How does Doerr write the chapters told from Marie-Laure's point of view?
options: Through diary entries she writes in braille during the siege
Through letters she sends to her father in his prison camp
Through the eyes of Etienne, who describes what she cannot see
Through sound, touch and smell, with very little that she sees
questions.explanation: Doerr builds Marie-Laure's world from textures, sounds and scents. Readers experience the city as she does, which makes her blindness a different way of perceiving, not an absence.

questions.stem: 'Is it right to do something only because everyone else is doing it?' Who asks this?
options: Jutta, questioning where Werner's choices are leading
Frederick, refusing an order from Commandant Bastian
Madame Manec, urging Etienne to resist the occupation
Marie-Laure, arguing with Etienne about the Germans
questions.explanation: Jutta's question goes to the heart of Werner's choices. He tells himself he has no choice, but the novel keeps asking whether going along with the crowd is ever an excuse.

questions.stem: Frederick tells Werner, 'Your problem, Werner, is that you still believe you own your life.' What does he mean?
options: That under the Nazi system Werner's choices are not truly his own
That Werner is selfish and cares only about his own future
That Werner is too proud to accept help from his friends at school
That Werner owes his place at the school to Frederick's family
questions.explanation: Frederick sees that the state claims the boys completely, and that Werner's belief in his own freedom is an illusion. The line also raises the question of how responsible Werner is for what he does.

questions.stem: Madame Manec tells Etienne, 'Doing nothing is as good as collaborating.' What idea does this express?
options: That ordinary people have no power to change the war
That staying passive under occupation helps the enemy
That open resistance is too dangerous for old men like Etienne
That neutral people will be punished once the war is over
questions.explanation: Madame Manec rejects Etienne's argument that it is safest to keep out of trouble. The line links to Werner, whose silence at Schulpforta is also a kind of collaboration.

questions.stem: The Frenchman's broadcast tells children, 'Open your eyes and see what you can with them before they close forever.' Why is the line important?
options: It reveals that the broadcaster is blind, like Marie-Laure
It is a coded message telling the Resistance to begin an attack
It sparks Werner's curiosity and urges readers to see clearly
It warns the children that the Germans are about to invade France
questions.explanation: The line captures the wonder the broadcasts give Werner as a boy. Later it becomes ironic, since Werner closes his eyes to what the regime does, and Marie-Laure, who is blind, sees more truly.

questions.stem: Werner's teacher Hauptmann repeats the maxim 'It's only numbers, cadet.' How does the line connect to the novel's ideas?
options: It shows the regime's genuine respect for Werner's mathematical talent
It shows how the regime reduces people to numbers, hiding the cost
It shows the novel's own view that science stands apart from politics
It shows Hauptmann's private kindness toward a struggling student
questions.explanation: Hauptmann wants Werner to treat his radio work as pure calculation. The maxim hides what the calculations are for: finding people who will be killed.

questions.stem: The narrator says, 'Radio: it ties a million ears to a single mouth.' What does this suggest?
options: That the Frenchman's science broadcasts reached only a few children
That Werner's skill lets him listen in on a million private conversations
That the Nazi regime used radio to spread one message to a whole nation
That radio let ordinary listeners answer back to their leaders at last
questions.explanation: The image shows radio's power to unite listeners behind a single voice. In Werner's Germany, that power serves propaganda, the darker side of the technology he loves.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the question 'Analyse how Doerr uses Werner to explore complicity in war.'?
options: Werner Pfennig is a German orphan who grows up in a mining town with his younger sister Jutta
This essay will discuss the character of Werner in the novel All the Light We Cannot See
All the Light We Cannot See is a novel by Anthony Doerr that won the Pulitzer Prize in 2015
Through Werner, Doerr suggests that staying silent in an unjust system makes a person part of its crimes
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the question and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without making an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Marie-Laure's chapters describe lots of sounds and textures.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: List more of the sounds Marie-Laure hears during the siege of the city
Retell what Marie-Laure does in each chapter, in the order it happens
Explain how sensory detail lets readers share her way of knowing the world
Add the page numbers where each of the sounds and textures appears
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the technique does and why it matters. Linking the sensory writing to how Marie-Laure perceives the world connects the detail to the novel's ideas about seeing.
